newsitem.title: USA: US bankers split on including commerce in reform.
newsitem.headline: US bankers split on including commerce in reform.

text.p: While the U.S. banking industry strongly supports Congressional efforts to tear down the legal barriers between banking and other financial services, it remains divided on the issue of allowing commercial firms into the business.

In testimony prepared for a hearing Tuesday on bank reform, William McConnell, president of the American Bankers Association, said his trade group has supported limited entry of non-financial firms into financial services.

On the question of removing all limits, however, "some bankers have indicated concerns ... particularly concerns about potential for concentration of resources," McConnell said in his prepared remarks.

"On the other hand, there are bankers who believe that the arguments for a more wide-open approach to the banking and commerce issue are persuasive," said McConnell, who is also chairman of Park National Corp.

Insurance companies and unitary thrifts, which can own or be owned by commercial companies, strongly favor allowing such combinations in the financial services reform legislation. Mutual funds also support the concept, but House Banking Committee chairman Jim Leach, along with smaller banks, unions and consumer groups, are opposed.
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, plotting the administration's position, is considering endorsing that aproach as well, people familiar with the plan said.
McConnell also said the ABA has not reached a firm position on another tough question: who should be the primary regulator of diversified financial services companies.

"In this area, the ABA has not taken a specific position at this point, and we do want to maintain flexibility to work with policy makers to determine the correct approach to holding company regulation," McConnell said.
